# Security

pysacd reads disc images and metadata that may come from anyone. This document records what
pysacd treats as untrusted, and how each kind of input is validated. The realistic adversaries
are corrupt images, buggy players and odd disc text, so the defence is input validation.
Containment against a hypothetical exploit (sandboxing, attackers on the LAN, hostile local
configuration) is out of scope; see [Extra isolation](#extra-isolation). Related issues: #12
(PS3 network protocol), #14 (engine, filesystem, HTTP, build), #17 (untrusted images).
To report a vulnerability, see [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

## Hostile text

A disc's TOC text (album and track titles, artists, publisher, catalogue numbers) is chosen by
whoever made the image, and MusicBrainz data is third-party. A crafted disc can put command
substitutions, option-like names, newlines or terminal escape sequences in those fields,
hoping that something downstream acts on them once pysacd has written them out. The
"something" might be a backup script running `tar *` as root, a shell loop over file names,
or the terminal displaying a name.

pysacd never executes text: it runs no shell, no `subprocess`, no `eval`. On top of that,
`pysacd.safetext` neutralises untrusted text everywhere pysacd writes or prints it.

| Where | Function | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| File and directory names (`convert`, and the `sacd_extract`-compatible names) | `name_component()`, `sbcompat._sanitize()` | control, bidi and zero-width characters removed; `` ` $ \| ; < > `` replaced with `_`; no component starts with `-` or `.`; `/` can't split a component; names stay inside the output directory |
| Tags (ID3, Vorbis), cue sheets, XML | `clean_text()`, `strip_controls()` | control, bidi and zero-width characters removed (XML keeps tab and newline, escaped); cue fields can't break onto a new line; XML is escaped |
| Terminal and logs (`-P`, `pysacd toc`, progress, warnings, errors) | `for_terminal()` | control characters are shown as escapes (`\x1b`), so text can't drive the terminal (colour, title, OSC 52 clipboard writes, keystroke injection) |

Characters that are common in real titles and only dangerous to scripts that already mishandle
names (`&`, `'`, `()`, `[]`, `!`) are kept. No sanitiser can make a name safe for a script that
`eval`s it. The rules above stop the attacks that work against *correctly written* scripts and
tools: option injection, newline splitting and terminal escapes. They also remove command
substitution, which real titles practically never contain.

### Differences from sacd_extract

The `sacd_extract`-compatible names follow sacd_extract's rules, plus the ones above. A disc
whose text contains `` ` ``, `$`, `;` or a leading `-`, or non-ASCII control or bidi
characters, therefore gets different names from `sacd_extract` (`Ke$ha` becomes `Ke_ha`). Every
other disc is byte-identical. That deviation is deliberate.

### Rule for contributors

Any new code path that writes or prints disc, MusicBrainz or network text must go through
`pysacd.safetext`. `tests/test_safetext.py` builds a disc with hostile titles and checks every
writer and printer. Extend it when you add one.

## Threat model

| Actor | Controls | Must not be able to |
|---|---|---|
| Whoever made a disc image | every byte of the image, including TOC text and audio frames | write outside the output directory, run commands, drive the terminal, crash or hang pysacd, corrupt another disc's output |
| A PS3 server, or anything on port 2002 | everything the client receives | the above, plus make the client allocate, write or wait without bound |
| A client of `ps3sim` | requests | read anything but the served ISO, crash the server, or hold it for ever |
| An on-path attacker | the unauthenticated, unencrypted PS3 traffic | anything a hostile server couldn't. Reading or altering sectors is possible and accepted (trusted networks only) |
| MusicBrainz and cover-art responses | tag text and images | the same as disc text (see #14 for HTTP limits) |

Output paths: each name component is neutralised (below) and capped at 240 bytes, `/` and `\`
can't split a component, and `..` can't appear as one. Lookalike slashes (U+2215, U+2044,
U+FF0F) are ordinary characters on every filesystem, so they can only make a name look
nested; they can't nest it. With `--portable-names` (always on Windows), trailing spaces and dots are removed and Windows
device names (`CON`, `NUL`, `COM1`, `COM¹`, …, with any extension) get a leading `_`.

## Hostile images

A disc image decides every length, count and position pysacd reads. Each one is bounded before
use, and a bad value makes pysacd skip the structure with a warning (TOC) or replace the frame
(audio), never read, allocate or write without limit. The limits sit far outside anything a real
disc uses: a survey of 110 discs found area TOCs of 5 to 41 sectors, at most 0.6 frames per
audio sector, and no track ending after its area's playtime.

| Value from the image | Bound |
|---|---|
| Area TOC size (master TOC) | at most 128 sectors, else the area is skipped |
| Area TOC and audio positions | read only where the image has sectors; an audio range that ends before it starts drops the area |
| Track start and duration | cut to the area's playtime, with a warning |
| Frames an extraction needs | at most 7 (the most a sector header can start) per audio sector the image really has, else the area fails with an error. Frames the disc lacks become silence, so without this a TOC could ask for hours of output from a few sectors |
| Track LSNs | only narrow where the engine reads, and only when every track's LSN lies inside the area's audio and the tracks are in order; otherwise the whole area is scanned |
| Text strings and items | 4096 bytes per string, item scans linear in the TOC size |
| Audio packets and frames | packets must fit their sector, a frame at most 64 KiB; an undecodable DST frame becomes 0x55 bytes and a missing frame becomes silence |
| Channel count | 1 to 6, else the engine refuses the area |

`tests/test_hostile_iso.py` checks this. `tests/sacdgen.py` builds about 95 hostile images:
broken, overlapping and truncated TOCs, absurd counts, timecodes and LSN ranges, bad text,
garbage, tiny, oversized and endless frames, and 2048/2054/2064-byte sector layouts with wrong
data offsets. Each image goes through every `pysacd-extract` mode (`-s`, `-p`, `-p -c`, `-e`,
`-I`, `-P`) and `pysacd convert` (DSF, FLAC, WAV), in-process. Each run must end in a clean
error or sane output: no other exception, no hang, nothing outside the output directory, no
partial file left behind, and no file larger than the image's sectors could hold. CI runs it
under ASan and UBSan. `PYSACD_HOSTILE=name,...` runs only the named images.

Where `sacd_extract` differs on such images: it writes a zero-length track as a DSF header
with no audio, while `pysacd-extract` stops with an error ("empty range") and `pysacd convert`
skips the track with a warning.

## Running as root

The engine parses attacker-controlled images, and an image that exploited a bug in it would
run with the privileges of whoever ran pysacd. As root, that's the whole machine.

- `pysacd convert` refuses to run as root. `--allow-root` overrides that, with a warning.
- `pysacd-extract` only warns, with one line on stderr and in the log. It is a drop-in for
  `sacd_extract`, which runs as root, and `sudo` is a common way to read `/dev/sr0`.
  Refusing would break scripts that work with `sacd_extract`.

For more isolation than an ordinary user account, see [Extra isolation](#extra-isolation).

## Extra isolation

pysacd's defence against hostile images is validating its input: bounded lengths and
allocations, the checks above, sanitizer CI and fuzzing. It doesn't sandbox itself. To process
images you trust even less, run it in a container with no network, the image mounted
read-only and only the output directory writable. For example, with any image that has
pysacd installed (shown as `IMAGE`):

```sh
podman run --rm --network none --userns=keep-id \
  -v /path/to/album.iso:/in.iso:ro,Z -v "$PWD/out":/out:Z -w /out \
  IMAGE pysacd-extract -2 -s -i /in.iso
```

## MusicBrainz credentials

ISRC submission (`pysacd submit-isrcs`, `--submit-isrcs`) is the only feature
that writes to a remote service, and it asks before every submission.

- **OAuth token:** `~/.config/pysacd/musicbrainz-token.json`, created with mode
  0600 and never through a symlink. It's refused if others can read it, and
  it's used only for the server it was issued by.
- **Passwords** (digest auth) are asked for each time or read from
  `PYSACD_MB_PASSWORD`. They're never written anywhere.
- **What's sent:** only ISRCs that pass validation (`CCXXXYYNNNNN`), with the
  recording ids from the matched release. Disc text is never sent.

## PS3 network protocol

The SACD Ripper protocol (`docs/ps3-protocol.md`) has **no authentication and no encryption**.
Real PS3s speak it as is, so pysacd can't change that. Anyone on the network path can read or
alter the sectors. Use it on trusted networks only. pysacd treats everything the server sends
as hostile:

- **Messages:** length-delimited fields are capped at one 512-sector read plus 1 KiB, and a
  message may have at most 16 fields.
- **Reads:** a reply must return between 1 and the requested number of sectors, with exactly
  that much data.
- **`DISC_SIZE`:** capped at 2^22 sectors (8 GiB), just above a dual-layer SACD, so a server
  can't make the client create an enormous sparse file.
- **TOC over the network:** areas whose TOC or audio lies outside the disc, or whose end comes
  before their start, are rejected as malformed. Fetch ranges are clamped to the disc.
- **Time:** each request has a deadline: the timeout (60 s) covers the whole response, not
  just each `recv()`, so a server can't trickle a reply a byte at a time. Reconnects are
  bounded (3 in a row, with backoff), and every successful reply moves the copy forward, so
  the total transferred never exceeds the requested ranges.
- **Reconnects:** a reconnect that reports a different disc size or master TOC fails the
  copy. A server that swapped discs (even another pressing with the same size) can't splice
  another disc into the file.
- **Temporary files:** the sparse ISO for a partial fetch is created with `mkstemp` (mode
  0600, unpredictable name) in the output directory. It is removed on success, on error and on
  Ctrl-C. A SIGKILL, or a SIGTERM with no handler, leaves a `.pysacd-remote-*.iso` behind.
  That is a known limitation.
- **Text on the disc:** it's still disc text. Names, tags and output are neutralised as
  described under [Hostile text](#hostile-text), and every output path stays inside the output
  directory.

`pysacd ps3sim` serves an ISO to anyone who can reach its port. It listens on `127.0.0.1` by
default, warns when given another address, and closes connections that stay idle for
`--idle-timeout` seconds (default 60), so one silent client can't hold the single connection
for ever.

## Fuzzing

`tests/test_fuzz.py` runs seeded mutation fuzzing on the Python code that parses untrusted
bytes:

- `decode_message`, on mutated and random byte streams delivered in random-sized chunks;
- the PS3 client (`open`, `size`, `read_some`, `close`), against mutated server responses
  and fields sent with the wrong wire type;
- `read_toc`, on images whose master or area TOC has been corrupted or truncated, followed by
  `needed_ranges()` on whatever parses;
- the `ps3sim` request handler, which must keep serving a well-behaved client afterwards.

The rule each target is held to: hostile input produces the module's own error
(`RemoteError`, `SACDError`, `EOFError`) or a sane result, never another exception, an
out-of-range value or a hang. It runs in the normal test suite (300 cases per target) and
reproduces from the seed in a failure. `PYSACD_FUZZ=N` runs N cases. Fixed when it was added
(the first two found by the fuzzer, the others by review and now covered by targeted cases):

- varints longer than 64 bits;
- a response whose data field isn't length-delimited;
- requests whose fields have the wrong wire type, which crashed the `ps3sim` handler;
- a track-text offset pointing past the end of the area TOC (now a warning, and the track
  keeps no text).

The native engine's parsers, the sector demuxer and the DST decoder, have libFuzzer
harnesses (`fuzz/`, built with ASan and UBSan). They run for 2 minutes per harness on pull
requests that touch the engine, and for 30 minutes weekly. Their seeds are synthetic frames
from the test encoder, covering every optional DST feature and the invalid frames. Crashing
inputs go into `fuzz/regressions/`, which `tests/test_fuzz_engine.py` replays on every test
run. The first long run (2026-10-28, 12 cores, 30 minutes) found nothing: about 1.8 million
DST frames and 0.4 million sector sequences, with no crash, sanitizer report or hang. The
end-to-end hostile-image corpus (see [Hostile images](#hostile-images)) runs every
extraction path on broken images, also under ASan and UBSan.
